title: name in an email local part
possessive with a straight apostrophe
text: Ana's contract and Ruiz's invoice are ready.

title: name joined with an underscore
why: An underscore counts as a word character, so the name is not a whole word. The leak check applies the same rule.

title: name in camel case
why: Camel case glues the two names into one word, which the whole-word rule skips.

title: name inside a hashtag
why: Joined lower-case names are one token, not a known form.

title: name in an unknown-host URL query
name right before an address in the middle of a sentence
text: Pagamos 247,80 € a Ana Ruiz <ana@gestoria.example> el lunes.

title: name from a header repeated bare in the body
text:
From: Pilar Gómez <pilar@estudio.example>

Hola Pilar, te escribe Gómez desde contabilidad.

title: greeting, sign-off and company with nothing in known
text:

text:

title: sign-off a blank line below its closing
text:

Kind regards,

Priya Raman

title: company in prose with a company word but no legal suffix
text: The retainer for Strand & Partners is due on Friday.
why: In prose only a legal suffix marks a company. A company word alone (Partners, Group, Studio) is too common in ordinary sentences to count, so a known list or a NER detector finds it.

title: sign-off name followed by a job title
text:
Thanks for the call.

Regards,
Odette Ashworth, CEO
Dorsal Partners

title: company named after a one-word private host
text:
From: ana@dorsal.example

The Dorsal team will call.
why: Only a host label of two to six hyphenated words marks a company in the text. A one-word label is too often an ordinary word to take as a name.
